title: “Is this a trap?”: Student teachers’ perceptions and adoption of GenAI in assessments in three teacher education courses
extended_summary:
This paper examines how student teachers perceive and adopt generative AI (GenAI) in university assessment when course policy explicitly permits appropriate use. The authors address a tension in higher education assessment: although GenAI can support learning and writing processes, it also raises concerns about assessment validity, academic integrity, and students’ fear of being accused of plagiarism. The study asks how students actually interact with GenAI in real assessment contexts, rather than in hypothetical scenarios, and how sociocultural and technological factors shape those interactions.

The approach studied was the integration of GenAI-permissive assessment policies into three teacher education courses. In all three courses, students were told they could use GenAI for assessments if they did not directly copy outputs and if they acknowledged use appropriately. The courses used mostly open-ended, reflective, and contextualised assessment tasks, such as reflective papers, group presentations, and case studies. Data were collected through an English-language survey of 85 students, 11 Cantonese semi-structured interviews, course materials, and 158 students’ GenAI-use declarations submitted with assignments.

The study was conducted at a research-intensive university in Hong Kong, involving one undergraduate teacher education course and two postgraduate diploma teacher education courses for pre-service and in-service teachers. The courses ran during September–November 2024; Course A lasted 7 weeks, while Courses B and C each ran for 9 weekly sessions. Participants were primarily student teachers, some of whom were already practising teachers.

The main conclusion is that allowing GenAI did not lead most students to use it: about 62.4% of survey respondents reported not interacting with GenAI for assessments. Those who did use GenAI mainly used it for proofreading, checking clarity, rewriting, or limited brainstorming, rather than generating assignment text. Students’ decisions were shaped less by technical barriers and more by assessment design, perceived learning value, self-confidence, inconsistent GenAI policies across courses, and fear of plagiarism accusations. The authors argue for consistent programme-level assessment policies, clearer communication with examples and feedback, and personalised or contextualised assessment designs that reduce uncritical reliance on GenAI.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools used for producing, revising, proofreading, checking, and brainstorming text or other assignment-related content; no single AI product was systematically evaluated.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in three teacher education courses were explicitly allowed to use GenAI for non-exam assessments, provided outputs were not copied directly and use was acknowledged. The study examined whether and how students used GenAI for assessment tasks such as reflective writing, group presentations, case studies, and term papers, and what sociocultural or technological factors shaped adoption.

findings.finding_summary: In a survey of students in three teacher education courses, 37.6% of respondents reported interacting with GenAI to help complete assessments, while 62.4% chose not to do so despite permitted use. Self-declarations submitted with assignments showed 28 of 158 students declared GenAI use, with discrepancies between anonymous survey responses and assignment declarations.
findings.measure: Student survey and assignment self-declaration of GenAI use in assessments

findings.finding_summary: Among students who reported using GenAI, the most common purposes were proofreading (14 students; 43.8% of GenAI users) and checking whether their writing was clear (11 students; 34.4%). Fewer students used GenAI for generating texts (6; 18.8%), rewriting texts following prompts (6; 18.8%), brainstorming (4; 12.5%), helping with pictures and diagrams (2; 6.3%), or getting general ideas from referenced papers (1; 3.1%).
findings.measure: Reported purposes of GenAI use in assessment completion

findings.finding_summary: Students who interacted with GenAI generally perceived it as helpful for completing assessments. Of the GenAI users, 8 students (25%) said it helped a great deal, 14 (43.8%) said it helped to some extent, and 7 (21.9%) said it helped a little.
findings.measure: Perceived effectiveness of using GenAI in assessments

findings.finding_summary: Overall assessment engagement was high across the three courses, with an average of 4.21 and SD = 0.46 on a 5-point Likert scale. A Mann–Whitney U test found no significant difference in assessment engagement between students who adopted GenAI and those who did not, U = 781.5, r = 0.07, p = 0.536.

Among students who did not interact with GenAI, the most frequently reported reason was preferring to work on the assessment by themselves (41 students; 77.4%), followed by concern about being accused of plagiarism (22; 41.5%). Other reasons included not wanting to use GenAI in any assessment (14; 26.4%), believing GenAI would not be helpful (13; 24.5%), and lacking necessary knowledge or skills (7; 13.2%).
findings.measure: Survey reasons for not interacting with GenAI in assessments

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods descriptive study using surveys, interviews, course materials, and self-declarations in three courses at one institution. It is not an RCT or QED and relies substantially on self-reported GenAI use, with acknowledged response-rate and declaration-consistency limitations.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports descriptive adoption, perceived helpfulness, and engagement findings, but no causal learning impact or academic achievement effect sizes. Impact on student outcomes is therefore unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative.
